excerpt: Columbia's highest-crash intersections in SCDPS data, including I-20 at Broad River Road and Malfunction Junction, plus South Carolina's rules for injury claims after an intersection crash.
keyTakeaways: Columbia sits at the crossroads of I-20, I-26, and I-77, and its interstate interchanges are its highest-crash locations: I-20 at Broad River Road logged 224 collisions in 2024, second-most of any intersection in South Carolina. SCDOT says the I-20/I-26 junction known as "Malfunction Junction" "no longer meets the demands of modern traffic" (I-26 between St. Andrews Road and I-20 carried 143,900 vehicles a day in 2025) and is rebuilding the corridor through its Carolina Crossroads program, with substantial completion expected in the mid-2030s. South Carolina's three-year statute of limitations (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) and modified comparative fault rule (less than 51% at fault) govern how victims recover compensation for injuries caused at these high-risk crossroads.

faqs.question: What is the most dangerous intersection in Columbia, SC?
faqs.answer: By state crash counts, it is I-20 at Broad River Road (US-176): 224 collisions in 2024, Richland County's highest and second-most of any intersection in South Carolina, after 229 in 2023 (SCDPS Traffic Collision Fact Book). The I-20/I-26 "Malfunction Junction" also ranked in both Richland's and Lexington's top five in 2024, with 219 collisions across the two counties. SCDOT's Carolina Crossroads program rebuilt the Broad River Road interchange, fully operational in fall 2025; the rebuild of the I-20/I-26 interchange itself is still in design.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a car accident lawsuit in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: Under S.C. Code § 15-3-530, you have three years from the date of your accident to file a personal injury lawsuit in South Carolina. Missing the statute of limitations typically means losing your right to compensation entirely.

faqs.question: Can I still recover compensation if I was partially at fault for a Columbia intersection crash?
faqs.answer: Yes. South Carolina follows a modified comparative fault rule that allows you to recover compensation as long as you are less than 51% at fault for the accident. Your total award is reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you are 25% at fault and your damages total $200,000, you would recover $150,000.

faqs.question: Why is the I-20/I-26 interchange called Malfunction Junction?
faqs.answer: "Malfunction Junction" is the local nickname for the I-20/I-26 interchange, a cloverleaf whose closely spaced ramps force drivers to weave across lanes in heavy traffic; the stretch of I-26 between St. Andrews Road and I-20 carried 143,900 vehicles a day in 2025. SCDOT says the interchange "no longer meets the demands of modern traffic" and is rebuilding the corridor through its Carolina Crossroads program, which it expects to substantially complete in the mid-2030s.

faqs.question: What should I do immediately after a car accident in Columbia?
faqs.answer: Call 911, seek medical treatment even if you feel fine, photograph the scene and all vehicle damage, collect witness contact information, do not admit fault, and contact a Columbia car accident lawyer before giving any recorded statements to insurance companies. South Carolina law requires you to notify police immediately after a crash that injures or kills anyone (S.C. Code § 56-5-1260). If no officer investigated a crash involving injury or $1,000 or more in property damage, the driver or owner must file a written report with the DMV within 15 days (S.C. Code § 56-5-1270).

faqs.question: Can I sue if dangerous road design caused my Columbia accident?
faqs.answer: Not for the design itself: South Carolina agencies are not liable for the design of highways (S.C. Code § 15-78-60(15)). But if a malfunctioning signal, missing sign, or road defect that the responsible agency knew or should have known about contributed to your crash, you may have a claim against the City of Columbia, Richland County, or the South Carolina Department of Transportation. Damages are capped at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence (S.C. Code § 15-78-120), and these governmental tort claims must be filed within two years — or three if a verified claim is first filed with the agency — under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-110), so consulting an attorney promptly is critical.
